Two months after Nooran’s death, his friends in Longueuil are seeking support and justice as the trauma lingers.

In memory of Nooran Rezayi, shot dead on September 21 by a police officer in Longueuil, about thirty people gathered at the site of the tragedy.

Le 22 novembre, j’étais à Longueuil, au: On November 22, I was in Longueuil, at the corner of Joseph-Daigneault Street, where the ceremony in honour of Nooran Rezayi took place. I stayed for the entire event to observe, listen and try to understand how the young people and loved ones are living through this collective grief. Several young people spoke to me briefly; others preferred to keep their distance. Their reserve is part of the story told here.
Les bénévoles du Centre Binetna, qui app: Volunteers from Centre Binetna, which provides listening and support to Nooran’s young friends and initiated the ceremony, agreed to explain to me their actions, their observations and their concerns about the psychological consequences for the young people. What they told me helped shed light on an important part of this article.
Pour documenter les mesures de soutien m: To document the support measures put in place since the tragedy, I contacted the City of Longueuil. The key elements of its response have been included in the article.
<strong>Rue Joseph-Daigneault, à Longueu: Joseph-Daigneault Street, in Longueuil – where Nooran Rezayi was shot by an officer of the Service de police de l’agglomération de Longueuil (SPAL). On Saturday, November 22, about thirty people gathered for a quiet ceremony. Amid silence, prayers and gestures of solidarity, a community tries to put a name to a trauma that is still raw.
<strong>Une fin d’après-midi glaciale, u: A freezing late afternoon, a grief that won’t pass
Il est un peu plus de 17 h. Le froid tom: It’s a little after 5 p.m. The cold drops all at once on this residential neighbourhood of Longueuil. The lighting is dim, almost nonexistent, and silhouettes slowly approach the street corner where Nooran fell.
Deux mois ont passé, mais pour les amis: Two months have passed, but for the teenager’s friends, the tragedy is still raw. They arrive in small groups. Some have their hoods up; others walk alongside an older figure. In front of the tree where Nooran collapsed, they light candles. The gestures are brief, hesitant. Words are even rarer.
La famille de Nooran est là aussi – ento: Nooran’s family is here too – surrounded, but silent. The family’s lawyer, M<sup>e</sup> Virginie Dufresne-Lemire, points out that no one can speak publicly while the investigation by the Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes (BEI) is ongoing. His mother stands back, her eyes reddened by days of tears, her face marked but dignified.
La cérémonie, organisée par le Centre Bi: The ceremony, organized by Centre Binetna, a Montréal organization offering therapeutic support, is meant to be simple and respectful. Funeral prayers are recited. A short speech is given. The minute of silence stretches a little longer than planned, as if everyone had drifted into a memory or a thought of Nooran. The ceremony ends after forty-five minutes. But the young people stay. They return in waves to the tree, stop there to pay their respects and leave without a word.
Karim Rachouane, 16 ans, serre les poing: Karim Rachouane, 16, clenches his fists in the pockets of his coat. He had known Nooran for several years. “He made everybody laugh,” the teenager says. “He wasn’t a troublemaker, you know, and when you found out he was in your class, you were happy. The teachers really liked him.”
La veille du drame, ils étaient ensemble: The day before the tragedy, they were together at the park nearby. The next day, Karim learned the news when he saw the police cars: “In my head, I was telling myself: ‘No way it’s him. They got the wrong person.’” But the media confirmed the information, he remembers. In shock, he went home, shut himself in his room and lay there without closing his eyes all night.
Aujourd’hui, Karim reçoit un soutien à l: Today, Karim receives support at school and regularly talks to a relative who works in mental health. But his anger remains intact. “I want justice to be done. We expect a harsh penalty for the cop, because Nooran was completely innocent, it was really just police brute force!” For Karim, the solution also involves more transparency: “We need bodycams. That way, it won’t happen again.”
Il hésite un instant quand on lui demand: He hesitates for a moment when asked whether he sees a racial issue in this tragedy. Then he says firmly: “Yes, 100%. […] Personally, I see a lot of racism in this. If it was a Québécois in that situation, nothing would have happened. The cops wouldn’t even have gotten out of the car. They would never have thought about pulling out a gun and shooting a 15-year-old.”
‍<strong>Un matin en cuisine, un soir en: ‍A morning in the kitchen, an evening in silence
« Ils ont tous mis la main à la pâte, ra: “They all pitched in,” says volunteer Sana Mansouri, whose little brother was close to Nooran. “Some of them had ideas to improve the recipe. You could see it was doing them good. A kind of pride.”
Mais dès que la conversation revient sur: But as soon as the conversation returns to her little brother, Sana’s tone changes. “It’s hard,” she says. “He has a much harder time communicating his emotions. There are effects on his grades, on his behaviour… You can tell it was a traumatic event for him; and I imagine for so many others.”
Pour elle, les répercussions de la mort: For her, the impact of Nooran’s death reaches far beyond the immediate circle of his friends. “It touched an entire community. A lot of young people were affected and kind of left to fend for themselves.”
Les familles, dit-elle, font ce qu’elles: Families, she says, are doing what they can. But the loneliness remains, especially since media attention has faded: “People talked about it a lot at first. Then it became a news brief.”
L’événement organisé ce jour-là vise don: The event organized that day is therefore meant to create a moment of gathering. “It’s hard to put words to what they’re going through. Sometimes actions help them more than words,” Sana adds.
L’activité de cuisine communautaire s’es: The community cooking activity took place during the day at the Longueuil youth centre, under the supervision of Centre Binetna workers.
Psychologue et fondatrice du centre, Ime: A psychologist and the centre’s founder, Imene Staali made it her mission to support Nooran’s friends starting the day after the tragedy. For her, the wounds left by the death of the young Rezayi run deep and are largely invisible in these young people. “[They] may get stomach aches without understanding why, have nightmares – they probably already do. These are young people who are losing their concentration at school, and we’re worried about whether they’ll stay in school or drop out. We’re afraid they’ll end up with substance use problems, we’re afraid for their health,” says M<sup>s</sup>. Staali.
Un ensemble de répercussions qui, selon: A set of repercussions that, in her view, are amplified by the lack of institutional recognition of what they’re going through: “IVAC (<l1>Indemnisation des victimes d’actes criminels</l1>, editor’s note) and CAVAC (<l2>Centre d’aide aux victimes d’actes criminels</l2>, editor’s note) don’t recognize police violence as a criminal act. So these young people don’t have access to those services.” And that’s where the centre steps in, M<sup>s</sup>. Staali insists, to fill that void and help them by offering care. “We want to show them that Nooran isn’t forgotten,” she adds. “That we continue to honour his memory, and also to respond to their needs.”
‍<strong>« On a besoin que les instituti: ‍“We need institutions to take a stand”
Interrogée sur les besoins de la communa: Asked about the community’s needs, Imene Staali maintains that one of the knots at the heart of the collective pain is tied to the silence of institutions. She says the community is waiting for a clear gesture, a statement that acknowledges the nature of what happened. “We need the City, the government, to denounce this act as police violence,” she says. She rejects the idea, often raised publicly, that “police work is complicated.” “It’s not complicated not to kill a 15-year-old!” she exclaims.
Selon la psychologue, une prise de posit: According to the psychologist, a public stand would have a healing effect. “We need them to speak out, to take a position. For the government to listen to the young people’s needs too. What are their needs? Let them listen…” she says.
Elle insiste autant sur l’écoute que sur: She stresses listening as much as support, but also reparation: reparations for a community marked by Nooran’s death, for his loved ones, for his friends. “The institutions must repair what happened. This affects an entire community, an entire ecosystem. Nooran’s friends need reparations.”
Pour elle, la réparation passe également: For her, reparation also involves symbolic gestures: “Can we ask for a mural? To rename a park? It will never bring Nooran back, but these are the beginnings of reparation,” the psychologist says.
Du côté de la Ville de Longueuil, le cab: On the City of Longueuil’s side, the office of Mayor Catherine Fournier says support measures were rolled out as soon as the tragedy was announced. An emergency unit was set up to coordinate interventions with the young people, in collaboration with the Centre de services scolaire Marie-Victorin, which mobilized psychologists and psychoeducators, according to a written response sent by the communications department.
La Ville de Longueuil dit avoir été réce: The City of Longueuil says it was recently informed of concerns about some young people who reportedly have not received the help they need. “Our teams are working with partners to make sure that every young person who expresses a need is taken care of,” the same communication states. Finally, the City says it wants to strengthen outreach initiatives with young people, and to that end it encourages students and their families to turn to their school’s administration for help. “The CSSMV assures us that any student who raises their hand to ask for support will be assisted.” We were unable to obtain confirmation or details of this initiative from the Centre de services scolaire Marie-Victorin, which did not respond to our emails.
De son côté, le Centre Binetna prévoit p: For its part, Centre Binetna plans to continue its support. “If they [the young people and their families] need us to come back every week, we’ll come back. Every month, we’ll hold a commemoration. We’ll be there,” concludes the centre’s director.
Autel de recueillement autour de l’arbre: A memorial around the tree where Nooran fell. Photo credit: Édouard Desroches
Tout au long de la soirée, les bougies c: Throughout the evening, the candles keep burning at the foot of the tree. The young people stay in tight little groups, speaking in low voices, rarely to others. They watch, they listen, but they exchange little with the adults present. A palpable reserve, almost a wariness, surrounds their conversations, as if speech, that evening, were possible only among themselves. In the accounts gathered throughout the evening, two feelings come up again and again: fear that this tragedy will happen again, and worry that the system will fail to hear the voices of these young people, who are asking for nothing more than to exist without violence.
Karim, lui, regarde longuement les flamm: Karim gazes at the flames for a long while. Before leaving, he adds: “I came because it’s important. We can’t forget.”
Deux mois après la mort de Nooran, son o: Two months after Nooran’s death, his shadow still hangs over Longueuil. The BEI investigation continues, the family awaits answers, and his friends are trying, as best they can, to find their way back to school. On this poorly lit street, the cold settles in. But around the tree, the candles keep burning, as if to make sure that here, at least, the light doesn’t go out.

Through commemorations, psychological support and calls for justice, Centre Binetna is supporting the young people affected by this tragedy, as institutions are called on to acknowledge and repair the impacts of police violence.
Plus tôt dans la journée, une trentaine: Earlier in the day, some thirty young people had gathered at the Longueuil youth centre. Under the supervision of a volunteer, they had made pâté chinois to be distributed at the Brossard mosque.
